Section One: Establishing the Rules for Practice, with Preface.
Now, a new garment without holes cannot be mended with thread;
one who has long cultivated pure goodness cannot be subjected to punishment.
When I was first at Fudu Temple in Jinling, I resided there.
Previously, when I first entered Tiantai, the various disciples who had come to study gathered together;
even then, there was no need for gentle words to encourage them in their spiritual practice,
let alone after the establishment of regulations to maintain discipline.
To enter the Tiantai contemplation as a late learner is like a newly tamed monkey or horse;
if it is not restrained by a bit and a halter, it will run wild.
Increasing day by day and month by month,
for the sake of accomplishment,
one loses two and gains one.
"The use of the willow whip to shame offenders was not intended as a hardship for them;
now, in instructing those who study,
I shall briefly present ten articles."
If, later on, obstacles arise, one must adjust [the practice] by increasing or decreasing it;
the assembly should collectively determine this.
First, as for individuals, their faculties and natures differ.
Some attain the Way by practicing alone,
while others achieve liberation by relying on the community.
If one relies on the community, they should cultivate the three types of practice.
First, sitting in meditation according to the hall;
second, performing repentance in a separate area;
third, attending to monastic affairs.
These three types of practitioners possess the full set of requisites— the three robes and six articles;
whichever one of these practices they follow, they may be accommodated.
If there is a deficiency in robes or clothing,
and there is not even a single row [of them], one shall not dwell together;
this applies to the monks residing in the second hall.
Originally, sitting in meditation during the four periods of the day and prostrating before the Buddha during the six periods were my constant duties;
these ten periods of meditation and prostration must never be omitted.
The separate practice of the *saṃghācāra* dharma is hereby concluded.
Beyond three days, one must immediately conform to the ten periods of the assembly.
If one fails to perform even one period of prostrations to the Buddha, one shall be penalized by performing three prostrations before the assembly as a confession.
If one completely fails to observe one of the six periods of worship,
the punishment is ten prostrations performed as a public confession before the assembly.
If one completely fails to observe all six periods, the punishment is one term of service as the *karmadāna* (rector).
The same applies to sitting in meditation during the four periods of the day.
If one removes obstacles that cause illness,
and first informs the administrative official (karmadāna), then one shall not be punished.
Third, regarding the practice of prostrating to the Buddha at the six times of the day:
the Great Sangha should wear the *saṃghāṭī* when entering the assembly.
If the robe lacks pleats or if it is like a seamless garment (*kaṣāya*), it is not permitted at all.
When the bell is struck three times for the early assembly, one should arrange the seats and take up the incense burner, kneeling alternately.
One must not recite until the chanting has begun,
and one must not engage in casual conversation before the *svādhyāya* (recitation of scriptures).
Prostrating with the head to the ground, snapping the fingers, and abruptly dragging the sandals back and forth in uneven intervals—
all such acts shall be punished by ten prostrations performed as a confession before the assembly.
This is the fourth point concerning the meaning of distinct practices.
Because they are lax while among the assembly,
they diligently cultivate the four kinds of samādhi;
yet, by merely resorting to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they do not accord with the intent of distinct practice.
Upon investigation, if the facts are established, the *vinaya-dhara* (rectifier) shall be punished once.
Fifth, the monks who serve as administrators (*karmadāna*) exist fundamentally for the purpose of establishing benefit.
On the contrary, they cause depletion and waste, carving away from the community to enrich themselves and acting out of personal favoritism.
If they unreasonably encroach upon even a hair’s breadth,
even if it is for communal use, they do not provide public disclosure.
Upon investigation, it was found that they were indeed different.
Regarding the second point, the sixth [rule], concerning eating at the proper time:
if one is not ill, or if being ill does not require lying down for an extended period.
Once the illness has been cured, all must leave the hall;
one must not request food and enter the assembly.
Regarding eating utensils, iron and ceramic are permitted for use.
Regarding the two vessels for incense oil, as well as the bowls, saucers, spoons, and chopsticks,
none of these may be made of bone, horn, bamboo, wood, gourd, lacquer, leather, or shell;
none of them are permitted to enter the hall.
Furthermore, one must not strike or touch one's own alms bowl;
nor should one make sounds while sucking or slurping, nor speak with food in the mouth;
nor should one seek out condiments or vegetables for oneself and take them privately.
To eat alone from among the assembly,
the offender shall be penalized with three prostrations and must perform repentance before the assembly.
Seventh, regarding the minor precepts for the Great Sangha:
Whether traveling near or far, whether within or outside the monastery,
one must under no circumstances steal, eat fish, meat, pungent vegetables, or wine,
nor eat at improper times.
Upon investigation, if it is found that they did not actually stop together,
except in cases where a patient is critically ill and medical treatment is required as advised by a physician,
then going outside the monastery to seek treatment shall not be punished.
The eighth name for the Saṃgha is "Harmony.
It is harmonious because of gentleness and patience;
it is unified because of righteousness and yielding.
One must not engage in disputes, raise one's voice, use foul language, or display agitated facial expressions.
Those who compete in such ways shall each be punished with thirty prostrations and perform repentance before the assembly;
those who do not respond shall not be punished.
Regarding those who strike one another with their hands or bodies:
regardless of whether the offense is minor or grave, they shall not remain together;
however, those who do not move their hands shall not be punished.
Ninth, if one commits a grave offense, they shall be dealt with according to the Vinaya;
if there is a false accusation,
the accused shall not be punished.
One who commits a false accusation does not share the same residence.
If the training has not yet been entered into when one passes by the host of the community,
it is not accepted because the training community has not yet incorporated him.
If one who calls himself a bhikṣu enters the assembly and comes to commit a grave offense or falsely accuse another,
he shall be punished as previously described.
The tenth [section], based on the sūtras, establishes the directions, views, ailments, locations, and medicines;
what benefit would there be in administering medicine when one has already vomited it up?
As for the nine preceding sections on prohibitions, permissions, and repentance:
Though you have repeatedly confessed, your lack of shame and remorse prevents you from reforming yourself.
Such a person is like one who has vomited up medicine; they should be expelled from the assembly.
However, if you are able to change your ways, your readmission shall be permitted hereafter.
If one commits various transgressions of the precepts and stubbornly refuses to repent,
this person is one who does not follow the proper way;
since they do not comply with the communal regulations, they shall not dwell together with the assembly.
2. Homage to the Dharma; Homage to the Dharma, Part Two, with Preface. This teaching is based directly upon the *Vibhāṣā* of Nāgārjuna and supplements the intent of various other sūtras.
[It is to be practiced] for one day and one night.
The practice of being concise and adapting to the occasion consists of three types: at dawn and noon, one performs a brief respectful salutation;
in the afternoon, one uses a respectful salutation with a brief recitation.
The first watch of the night is used entirely for this;
at noon, ten Buddhas represent the middle watch;
and in the last watch, one performs universal prostrations.
With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
I solemnly uphold incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma.
May these clouds of incense and flowers...
Pervading the realms of the ten directions,
in each and every buddha-field,
there is adornment with immeasurable fragrances.
Fully endowed with the bodhisattva path,
they accomplish the fragrance of the Tathāgata;
having made offerings, they practice the Way according to the Dharma.
Having completed the circumambulation, he paid homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem and offered praises and prayers for the Buddha.
The prayer went as follows:
"His form is like Jambu-river gold."
His face surpasses the full moon in purity;
the radiance of his body and the brilliance of his wisdom illuminate without limit.
He crushes the hosts of Māra’s enemies and skillfully transforms all humans and devas;
he boards the vessel of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Able to deliver those who are difficult to deliver,
one attains non-retrogression upon hearing his name;
for this reason, I prostrate in homage.

One should praise the Buddha’s merits for the sake of the devas, nāgas, and dragon kings of the three realms, the state, the seven ancestral temples, the monastics, parents, donors who have built monasteries, and all enemies and kin alike;
may they all realize True Suchness together and attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Elder should speak with mastery through the power of wisdom.
Homage to all Buddhas, Vairocana, who pervade the Dharma-realm and dwell eternally in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
Homage to all Buddhas, Rocana, who pervade the Dharma-realm and dwell within the Lotus-Treasury Ocean.
Homage to Śākyamuni of the Sahā world and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Homage to the Buddha Candanaśrī of the world Abhirati in the southern direction, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Homage to the Buddha Amitābha of the world named Sukhāvatī in the western direction, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Homage to the Tathāgata Lakṣaṇaguṇa of the Akṣobhya World in the north, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharmadhātu.
Homage to the Buddha Aśokaguṇa of the Candraprabhā World in the southeast, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharmadhātu.
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnadatta of the world Viśvarūpa in the southwestern direction, and to all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm.
Homage to the Tathāgata Guṇakūṭa of the world Viśvaghosa in the northwestern direction, and to all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm.
Homage to all Buddhas who pervade the dharma-realm, the Buddhas of the practice of the three vehicles in the world of Peace and Security in the northeast.
Homage to all Buddhas who pervade the dharma-realm, the Tathāgatas of Virtuous Radiance in the vast world below.
Homage to the Buddhas who pervade the entire dharma-realm, including the Buddha Vistīrṇaguṇasāgara of the Candravatī World in the zenith.
Homage to the Buddhas who pervade the entire dharma-realm, including the Buddha Vipaśyin beneath the Aśoka Bodhi tree.
Homage to the Tathāgata Śikhin beneath the Pāṭalī tree, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Homage to the Buddha Viśvabhū beneath the Śāla grove, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Homage to the Buddha Krakucchanda beneath the Śirīṣa tree, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Homage to the Buddha Kanakamuni beneath the Udumbara tree, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Homage to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa beneath the Kakubha tree and to all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Homage to the Tathāgata Maitreya beneath the Nāgapuṣpa tree and to all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
I pay homage to the reliquaries, images, shrines, and precious stupas.
I pay homage to the twelve divisions of the sutras, the pure and wondrous Dharma.
I pay homage to the Sangha of all noble and holy ones of the three vehicles who have attained the Way.
For the sake of Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes of divine attendants, and all the celestial deities who protect the nation and uphold the Dharma,
may you exercise sovereign power and freely manifest the Buddha-work.
We pay homage to all the eternally abiding Buddhas.
For the sake of all the dragon kings and others,
may the wind and rain fall in their proper seasons so that all living beings may receive nourishment.
I pay homage to the eternally abiding Buddhas.
For the King of Mount Tiantai, his retinue, and all the hidden deities of the peaks, foothills, forests, and wilds—
may you secretly bestow blessings upon this monastery to bring about great benefit.
We pay homage to the eternally abiding Buddhas.
For the sake of the seven ancestral temples and the sacred spirits of Emperor Wu Yuan and Empress Dowager Yuanming,
we pray that their divine souls may roam the Pure Lands and enter the Dharma-clouds.
We reverently pay homage to all the Buddhas who abide eternally.
For the service of Your Most Honored and Holy Majesty:
we pray that the precious calendar may extend far and wide, and that the heavenly mandate may endure forever;
that Your Compassion may encompass the myriad nations and rescue all beings of the four modes of birth.
Homage to all Buddhas, who abide eternally.
For the person of the Empress,
may she be adorned with a hundred blessings and protected by a thousand sages.
I pay homage to all the Buddhas who abide eternally.
For the sake of His Imperial Highness the Crown Prince,
I pray that the state may be preserved, the people brought to peace, and blessings extended for ten thousand generations.
I pay homage to all Buddhas, who abide eternally.
For the sake of the ministers, officials, and the five ranks of the imperial court,
I pray that you shall assist and support the Royal House, fulfilling every duty with utmost integrity.
I pay homage to all Buddhas who abide eternally.
For the sake of my parents from past lives, my teachers and monks of successive generations, and the fourfold assembly of donors— grateful for their twofold kindness of wealth and Dharma—
I pray that they may swiftly transcend the sea of suffering and forever emerge from the river of craving.
Homage to all Buddhas, who abide eternally.
For the sake of the deceased patron and benefactor who provided the foundation for this work, and for the sake of transforming the assembly of monks and others:
may the six perfections be swiftly perfected and the seven riches be fully attained.
I pay homage to all the Buddhas who abide eternally.
For the Prefectural Governor, the Magistrate, the officials of the Six Ministries, the Commandant of this County and Town, and the men and women of the five districts:
may there be auspicious winds and timely rains, and may the entire realm enjoy abundance and peace.
I pay homage to all Buddhas, who abide eternally. For all instances of encroachment, injury,
or harm committed since the founding of this monastery— including the clearing and cultivation of fields and gardens, the construction of kitchens and granaries,
and all movements and activities— I pray that upon passing away, I may return to the truth and remain free from retribution in the future.
I pay homage to all Buddhas who abide eternally.

For the sake of realizing the equality of the nature of consciousness regarding enemies and kin within the Dharma-realm, I sever the three obstacles and, with sincere heart, repent and confess my transgressions.
There is nothing unknown to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions.
I now confess before you all my dark and evil deeds—
nine types in three sets of three—
all arising from the three afflictions.
Whether committed in this present life or in previous lives, I now repent of all my transgressions.
Should there be any karmic retribution due to me in the three evil realms,
may I repay it within this present life and not enter those evil paths.
Having received the repentance, one prostrates before all Buddhas and,
with a sincere heart, entreats all Buddhas of the ten directions who have currently attained the Way:
"I now request you to turn the Wheel of Dharma to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
To all Buddhas of the ten directions,
should they wish to relinquish their life-span,
I now prostrate with my head at their feet.
Exhorting [the Buddhas] to remain for a long time,
and having made this exhortation, one pays homage to all the Buddhas and, with a sincere heart,
rejoices in all merit arising from body, speech, and mind— namely, the virtues of giving, maintaining the precepts, and practicing meditative concentration.
All ordinary beings rejoice in accordance with all those who have studied the three vehicles in the past, future, and present, and who have accomplished the three vehicles.
Having rejoiced, they pay homage to all Buddhas.
With a sincere heart, I dedicate all my merit, unifying it entirely for the sake of all sentient beings.
I thus correctly dedicate it toward the Buddha-way; my transgressions should likewise be repented in this manner.
Exhorting [the Buddhas] to teach, rejoicing in merit, and dedicating it toward enlightenment;
having thus dedicated it, one pays homage to all Buddhas and makes aspirations with a sincere heart.
May all sentient beings alike resolve to attain bodhicitta,
and with their minds focused,
constantly keep in mind all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, I vow that all sentient beings shall forever shatter all afflictions and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature,
just like Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) and others.
Having made the vow, take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas.
Recite this universally;
once the recitation is finished, one should maintain silence.
Brahmā has already repented.
Having repented, he prostrates before the Buddha with reverence and takes refuge in the Buddha, making this aspiration for all sentient beings: may they [attain] suchness.
Having realized the Great Way and resolved upon the Unsurpassed Mind, one takes refuge in the Dharma;
may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, so that their wisdom is like the ocean.
One takes refuge in the Sangha; may all sentient beings...
May they govern the great assembly with harmony and unimpeded ease.
May all sentient beings purify their three karmas.
I reverently uphold the Honored One’s teachings.
I pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of noble sages.
Following this, having finished reciting the verses according to the occasion, I shall now announce the *cāturvārṣika* (the invitation for criticism).

3. Universal Prostration Dharma. Universal Prostration Dharma, Chapter Three. All acts of reverence, incantations, and aspirations are as previously described. One universally prostrates before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time at the site of the tranquil extinction of Vairocana Buddha.
I universally pay homage to Vairocana Buddha in the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.
I universally pay homage to Vairocana Buddha in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.
I universally pay homage to the Lokeśvararāja Buddha on Mount Pāṇḍuka in the Yāma Heaven among all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.
I universally pay homage to the Lokeśvararāja Buddha in Tuṣita Heaven among all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.
I universally pay homage to the Buddha Vairocana in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations among the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time;
I universally pay homage to the Buddha Vairocana in the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall where the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time have gathered again.
I universally prostrate before the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time; before the Bodhisattva Sudhana and Vairocana Buddha within the Jeta Grove;
and before Vairocana Buddha of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, as manifested in the seven locations and nine assemblies throughout the ten directions and three periods of time.
I universally pay homage to the Vairocana Buddha of the Treasury of Immovable Precepts of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time throughout space.
I universally pay homage to the Vairocana Buddha of the Treasury of Immovable Samādhi of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time throughout space.
I universally prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, to the Akṣobhyajñānagarbha Vairocana Buddha.

I universally prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, to the Vairocana Buddha who, having attained bodhi by taking refuge in the Buddhas, possesses a virtuous mind that never regresses.

I universally prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; I take refuge in the Dharma of Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and enter the gate of the Great Dhāraṇī, Vairocana Buddha.

I universally prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; I take refuge in the Saṃgha that has ceased all disputes and enter the ocean of Great Harmony, Vairocana Buddha.
May all sentient beings purify their three karmas and reverently uphold the Honored One’s teachings.
Homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Sages.

The Fourth Ritual for the Repentance of Invoking Avalokiteśvara. A direct record of the essential matters; the specific instructions for visualization and wisdom are set apart from the rest of the text. As the Sutra says:
For the three-week period and the seven-seven-day period,
one should observe the six fast days; at the commencement, one ought to solemnly adorn the *dharmadhātu-maṇḍala*,
smearing the ground with fragrant mud and suspending various banners and canopies.
Place the image of the Buddha facing south, and the image of Avalokiteśvara separately facing east toward the sun.
Set aside willow branches and pure water;
burn incense and scatter flowers.
There shall be ten practitioners.
Having returned, they should sit on the ground facing west;
if the ground is low or damp, they should place low-legged stools upon it.
One should change into clean robes;
upon entering or exiting from the left or right after finishing the ritual bathing, one should put on the clean garments.
One should offer worship with all one's strength every single day.
If you are unable to provide [all these],
at the very least you must not fail to offer incense and perform the ritual of settling the altar.
Each person should hold an incense burner and focus their mind with single-minded devotion.
Facing that western direction, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground,
and let those skilled in clear vocalization chant:
"With single-minded devotion, we pay homage to the Original Teacher, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni."
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored One Amitāyus of the Western Quarter.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World-Honored Ones of the Seven Buddhas.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the *Dhāraṇī for Eliminating and Subduing Poisonous Harm*, the *Dhāraṇī for Destroying Obstacles of Evil Karma*, and the *Six-Syllable Chapter*.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the Honored Dharmas of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Sangha of Worthy and Holy Ones, consisting of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Having completed the prostrations, burn incense, scatter flowers, and speak these words.
Then, all these members of the assembly shall each kneel upon their right knees.
Diligently holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma,
honoring the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm.
Having completed these mental recollections, utter these sincere words aloud.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions,
making offerings to all Buddhas.
The Honored Ones, the Bodhisattvas,
and the immeasurable assembly of Śrāvakas,
by means of their arising luminous terraces, [manifested this].
Beyond the boundless limits,
throughout infinite Buddha-fields,
they perform the work of Buddhas.
It universally perfumes all sentient beings,
causing them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta;
having completed the offerings, one should then turn toward the western direction.
Sit in the full lotus posture and bind the mindfulness to counting the breaths,
ensuring that the mind does not become distracted.
Do not count the wind, panting, or gasping.
For the sake of sentient beings,
after completing ten recitations in the duration of ten moments of thought,
one next recollects the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Seven World-Honored Buddhas.
The true mark of the form-body is a wondrous body like empty space.
Furthermore, one should maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
when forming this thought, it is as if one were in the first dhyāna.
Having maintained this recollection for a long time, he slowly and serenely awakens.
One person prepares the incense and lamps,
while each person kneels facing one another to perform the invocation.
With single-minded devotion, recite "Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha" three times. Having completed the invocation, invite the Triple Gem previously venerated.
Once the invitation is finished, say: "I have now prepared willow twigs and pure water."
I only pray that you, out of great compassion, will take pity on me and accept me;
say this three times. Next, recite the names of the Three Jewels and the name of Avalokiteśvara three times.
Then, join your palms and recite the verse.
"May you deliver me from this suffering and calamity.
After the four long prose passages following the verse,
one next recites the mantra for subduing and eliminating poison and harm.
After reciting the mantra, repeat the following seven lines of scripture either three times or seven times;
then further invoke the names of the Triple Gem and recite the *Pò èyè zhàng tuóluóní zhòu* (Dhāraṇī for Destroying Obstacles of Evil Karma).
Next, further invoke the names of the Triple Gem.
Having finished reciting the six-syllable mantra,
one should personally employ the power of one's own wisdom to lay bare and repent of [one's transgressions].
One who has violated the practice of the Brahma-faring and committed the ten unwholesome deeds may, by sweeping away filth and impurities, once again attain purity.
Next, one should make vows; having completed the vow of repentance, [one proceeds].
With single-minded devotion,
perform prostrations to the Triple Gem invited above.
Having completed the prostrations, practice the Way according to the Dharma.
After completing three or seven circumambulations, perform the threefold refuge.
Once the refuge has been completed, have one person ascend a high seat to chant and recite the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*.
In the early morning and during the first watch of the night, one should perform the method of supreme giving;
at other times, one should practice seated meditation and pay homage to the Buddha according to the regular rules.
This constitutes the regimen for one day and one night.
This continued likewise for the second, and so on up to the seventh seven-day period. 5.
The Ritual of Repentance of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Chapter Five: A Direct Record of the Events. The Contemplative Wisdom is set apart; the remaining text adorns the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).
Set up a separate platform for the recitation of the sutra,
arranging banners, flowers, and other offerings according to the aforementioned ritual.
Install the seat of Puṇyadharā (Gongde Tian) to the left of the Buddha’s seat.
If the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) is spacious, further arrange a great seat for Mahāprajñā.
The seats of the Four Heavenly Kings are placed to the right.
Incense should be burned and flowers scattered upon each of these seats.
Exert all effort in preparing fruits and vegetables;
furthermore, set aside a separate platter of assorted fruits and vegetables,
intending to scatter them in all directions.
On that day, one should bathe and put on new, clean robes.
As the Sūtra says:
"For seven days and seven nights, one should observe the six fast days."
On the first day at noon, each person shall hold an incense burner.
One person shall chant:
"All pay homage with reverence."
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the eternally abiding Three Jewels of the ten directions.
Each member of this assembly shall kneel in turn,
solemnly holding incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma.
Having silently completed the mental offering,
he spoke these words:
"May these clouds of incense and flowers..."
"Pervading the realms of the ten directions.
Having spoken thus according to the aforementioned method:
One should perform the invocation:
with single-minded devotion, invoke the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha;
with single-minded devotion, invoke the Buddha Akṣobhya of the East.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Ratnaketu of the South.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Amitāyus of the West.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Sutejoghoṣa of the North.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the World-Honored One Ratnakusumavaiḍūrya;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Ratnavijaya;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Vimalajvalanaratnāvabhāsasvararāja.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Golden Flame Radiance;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Treasury Illumined by a Hundred Golden Radiances;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha Golden Mountain Jewel Canopy.
With single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha of Golden Flower and Blazing Radiance;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha of the Great Torch;
with single-minded devotion, I entreat the Buddha of Precious Marks.

*Guoqing Bailu*, Volume Four. Biographical Chronology and Deeds of the Great Dhyāna Master Zhizhe. In the fourth year of the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the year Wuyou (489 CE), the Great Dhyāna Master was one year old. His father’s surname was Chen.
Kaiguo Hou was a native of Huarong in Jingzhou.
His mother, Lady Xu,
conceived after dreaming that she swallowed a white rat amidst clouds of incense.
At birth, divine light filled his room;
he had double pupils in each eye.
When he reached the age of seven, he delighted in visiting monasteries.
The monk orally transmitted the "Universal Gate Chapter" (Pumenpin) once;
as for the other passages he had not heard, [the boy] was able to understand them on his own.
His parents did not permit him to go there frequently.
In the first year of the Chengsheng era of Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty,
at the age of fifteen, he wished to leave the household life,
but his parents would not permit it.
He then carved a sandalwood image and performed rituals and recitations for one day.
While he was prostrating before the Buddha, he had a vivid dream in which a mountain stood over the great ocean;
a monk atop it beckoned to him with his hand.
In the first year of the Shaotai era of Emperor Jing of the Liang dynasty,
at the age of eighteen, after he had completed the mourning period for his parents,
he resolutely requested permission from his elder brother to leave the household life.
He then took the monk Faxu of Guoyuan Temple in Xiangzhou as his teacher;
his name was Zhiyi and his courtesy name was De'an.
This was the first year of the Yongding era of Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty.
At the age of twenty, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Under the guidance of Vinaya Master Huikuang, he became thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka;
however, prior to receiving full ordination, [he had already studied it].
Having previously studied the Vaipulya sutras under masters from whom he received instruction,
at the age of twenty-three, in the first year of the Tianxi era of Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty,
he relied upon Master Si at Mount Dasu in Guangzhou.
The Master recognized this as being the same assembly on Vulture Peak and revealed it as the Bodhimanda of Samantabhadra;
for the second seven-day period, he recited the Lotus Sūtra.
He attained profound and great enlightenment.
In the first year of the Guangda era of Emperor Feidi of the Chen dynasty,
at the age of thirty, he took leave of his teacher and departed for Jinling.
He resided at Waguan Temple for eight years,
where he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Shichidi Chanmen* (The Stages of Meditation),
and the *Fahua Xuanyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra).
In the seventh year of the Taijian era of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty,
at the age of thirty-eight, he entered Tiantai; however,
by imperial decree from Emperor Xuan, he was not permitted to remain there.
Initially, he stayed at Shiqiao and then moved to Fulong.
The following year, he subdued demons atop Huading Peak.
This was in the ninth year of the Taian era.
At the age of forty,
Emperor Xuan issued an imperial edict bestowing upon him Xiu Chan Temple.
This was in the thirteenth year of the Taijian era.
At the age of forty-four,
he lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
A fisherman relinquished his fishing nets, and [the Master] established a pond for the release of living beings (*fangsheng chi*).
The following year, Prince Yongyang requested that he lecture.
In the second year of Emperor Shao’s Zhide era,
at the age of forty-eight, he departed in accordance with an imperial decree.
In the Taiji Hall of Jinling, a Great Debate was convened and the *Renwang Jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) was expounded;
in the following year, the Crown Prince received the precepts.
In the first year of the Zhenming era,
at the age of fifty, he lectured on the Lotus Sūtra at Guangzhai Temple in Jinling.
At that time, Zhang’an was twenty-seven years old;
he had only recently begun to listen to the scriptural text.
This was the ninth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
At the age of fifty-two,
while in Jingzhou after the fall of the Chen dynasty, he had a dream that moved him to settle at Mount Kuang.
The following year, the Emperor of the Sui dynasty issued an imperial inquiry.
At the age of fifty-four,
the Prince of Jin invited him to Yangzhou.
In the eleventh month, he conferred the precepts upon the Prince of Jin, after which he was formally titled Zhizhe (the Wise One).
At the age of fifty-five,
he was able to travel to Jingzhou and Xiangzhou.
After passing through Mount Kuang once more, he completed his summer retreat there.
He arrived at the pond first.
At the age of fifty-six, he reached Jizhendi'en in Jingzhou and founded Yuquan Temple.
In his fifty-seventh year, having received the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) from Zhang’an,
he lectured on the *Mohe Zhiguan* at Yuquan Temple.
At the age of fifty-eight, he traveled from Jingzhou to Jinling.
At the request of Prince Jin, he composed a commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
In the spring of his fifty-ninth year, he returned once more to Tiantai.
In the winter of the following year, the Prince of Jin sent a letter summoning him with utmost sincerity.
At the age of sixty, he went to the summons and, before the stone statue at Xinchang,
sat upright and entered nirvana.
This was on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, during the hour of Wei (1–3 p.m.).
From the time of his parinirvāṇa until the twelfth year of the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty, the year of Yisi (1185).
